utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. It has been a while since we were in court. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Is the Defence ready to call its witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We are, Your Honours. We do also have a preliminary matter that I forgot to bring to the attention of the court officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's in relation to the e-mails I sent last week and yesterday as to some additional documents. So I did want to put on the record that the statement taken by the Karadzic Defence, which is our 1D3876, has several documents that are referenced and used in the statement which have not been previously identified or assigned 65 ter numbers. Thus, I take the opportunity to update that the document that is identified in footnote 52 of Witness Demurenko's statement, and in the footnote that's Karadzic P150, is already on our list for this witness and it is Exhibit D138 in the Mladic case. Further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic is speaking aloud, which he is supposed not to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Further, ERN R014-8176, cited in paragraph 24 of the statement, has been uploaded as 65 ter number 1D5967, and we would seek leave of the Court to add that to the 65 ter list of exhibits and the list for this witness. Additionally, Karadzic Exhibit P1960, cited in paragraph 50 of the Demurenko statement, was not identified on our table of concordance. That is already in evidence in our case as Exhibit D139. And we have Karadzic 65 ter number 1D26663, cited in paragraph 58 of the Demurenko statement, that also did not have a 65 ter number on our list. It has been uploaded as 1D5968, and we would seek leave of the Court to add that to the 65 ter list and for the witness. And then we have another Karadzic 65 ter number, 21618, cited in paragraph 70 of the Demurenko statement. That is already in our case Mladic 65 ter number 19020, and we put that on the record. And then we have ERN 07050079, referenced in paragraph 135 of the Demurenko statement, and that one did not have a 65 ter number. It has now been uploaded under Mladic 65 ter number 1D5969, and we would ask for that also -- to have leave to add that to the 65 ter exhibit list and for the list for this witness. And then we have two items that were sent along with the proofing note. They are 1D5970, which is the ICRC Martens reading, and 1D5971, which was a photograph, and we would likewise seek leave of the Chamber to add those to the list and to use with the witness. And I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you referred to paragraph 50 of the statement of Witness Demurenko. I don't find any number in paragraph 50. Can you check that again or help me to find it? Are you referring to the footnote 54?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I believe I'm referring to -- let me just double-check. It will appear that it is the footnote 54, which is then in relation to the tail-end of paragraph 50, which is found on the top of page 20 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Therefore, you should have said, yes, it is footnote 54.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I should have, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Only there the number appears.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, several requests for adding documents to the 65 ter list. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With respect only to the issue of adding, leave to add, no, we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then leave is granted to add them. Mr. Ivetic, apart from these matters are you ready to call the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We are ready to call the witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When the witness will join us, this gives me an opportunity to welcome the Russian interpreters. I do understand that the witness does speak English, but that if he speaks Russian, that at least we have the assistance, the highly appreciated assistance of Russian interpreters. Just for me to know, the Russian interpretation will be on what channel?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Russian interpretation will be on channel 7, into Russian. The interpretation into English will be on channel 4 as usual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And interpretation, if the witness would like to hear Russian interpretation of the questions, it would be on?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It will be channel 7, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so we should read Dutch -- "Russian" for Dutch on our screens. Good morning, Mr. Demurenko, I assume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Demurenko. Mr. Demurenko, before we start I'd like to ask you what language you preferably would use. Is that your own language, Russian, because we have Russian interpretation, or would you, since we know that you understand and speak English, or would you rather use the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would prefer to speak Russian, because there are important details and I could miss them if I spoke English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're perfectly free to choose your own language. Then you will give your testimony in Russian and the questions will be translated to you, interpreted into Russian. You'll now first be examined by Mr. Ivetic. One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I haven't introduced you yet. That's what I'll now do. Mr. Demurenko, you'll first be examined by Mr. Ivetic. You find Mr. Ivetic to your left, standing. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. And could I also ask you, because we have read your statement, which will soon be tendered, I take it, Mr. Ivetic, to focus very much on what the question is. If any further details are needed, then you'll be asked to give such details, but could you please start with focusing on exactly the question that's put to you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I would first ask that you introduce yourself by giving your full name and surname so that it can be recorded in the record.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: My name is Andrey Vladimovic [phoen] Demurenko, reserve colonel of the Russian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I can ask that we take a look at 1D03876 in e-court, and I have a paper copy of the same, with the assistance of the usher, that we can show to opposing counsel and then to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I think Mr. Mladic is seeking your attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm still waiting for the document on the screen, Your Honours. I hope I'm not the only one that is dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now we have it on everyone's screens. And, sir, looking at the first page of this amalgamated witnesses statement, do you remember giving a statement to Marko Sladojevic of the Karadzic Defence team as is set out in the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can turn to the last page both in e-court and in the hard copy, on this page we see a signature and a handwritten date of 13 October 2012. First of all, sir, do you recognise whose signature appears on this page?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I do. It's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And does the date that is written on here correspond with your recollection of when this statement was signed by you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to review with me in the past few days this whole statement to check if everything is accurate?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would propose that we go to page 2 of the statement and look at paragraph 3 of the same, which appears at the top of the page or -- the second half of paragraph 3 appears at the top of the page. And here, beginning on the second line down from the top -- or actually, let's start from the beginning. It says: "Naturally I am familiar with the entire arsenal that was at the disposal of the units that I just enumerated in my previous answer. All the infantry weaponry, including, 155-millimetre howitzers and machine-guns of all calibres, 62 -- sorry, 60, 82, 120-millimetre." Sir, are you talking about machine-gun calibres here or something else?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: In this specific case, it's an enumeration of calibres of machine-guns and the first figure refers to a howitzer. That's not a machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I note that you left out the words "all the artillery" in your quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. You are correct. You are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we cut -- try to cut this short. When you talked about 60-, 82-, and 120-millimetres, what kind of weaponry were you referring to? Machine-guns or anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, in my answer I was enumerating the weapons that I'm familiar with in the unit that I commanded, and these calibres were for mortars. The first one, 150, is a howitzer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now if we could turn to page 46 of the statement in both the e-court and hard copy, and I'll ask that we look at paragraph 107 of the same. And, sir, here it says, and I will just the quote part that is your answer, which is the fourth line down from the beginning of that paragraph: "A. I don't see where the problem is. You just draw a line from a possible firing location, or, rather - interpreter's correction - from a possible site of explosion and then you draw a line to a possible firing location. We have in the military very precise instruments, such as GPS and some other instruments, which can calculate down to a millimetre the location, instruments such as laser devices, and so on." First of all, when you say that in the military you have very precise instruments, such as GPS and other instruments which can calculate down to a millimetre, what other instruments did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I had in mind an artillery compass.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can look at the continuation of that paragraph, and it's the last line on this page, that reads: "Q. And at that time you had a GPS?" And if we could turn to the next page, it reads: "A. We have always had such a device for orientation, ever since the Americans put it in use. It's a universal military system." Sir, could you clarify for us if in relation to the investigation for Markale, in doing that investigation did you and your staff use GPS or some other instrument.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: No, at that time neither I nor my subordinates had any GPS systems or the Russian variant. We used what we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And could identify what it was that you used that you had?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The artillery compass, as I said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 72 of the statement in both the hard copy and in e-court, and in relation to the part on the bottom half of the page that relates to the sitrep that is in the document 1D28136, 5 June 1995. And at the bottom of the page, you have a comment about this document, and you say: "I completely agree that various national units within the UNPROFOR fought together against the Bosnian Serbs." And what I'd like to ask you, is it national units within UNPROFOR fighting together with themselves or with somebody else against the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I meant the units making part of the peacekeeping contingent, such as the Pakistani units.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with whom were they fighting together, these units that you identify against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Well, fighting is perhaps not the right word, but it was often obvious that the efforts made against Bosnian Serbs were made not only on the part of the Bosniaks but also some UNPROFOR units jointly with the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And, sir, apart from these corrections and clarifications that we have just gone through, do you stand by the remainder of the written statement as being true and correct to the best of your information?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it was accurate. It's a different matter that sometimes I have to spell out my various answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, if I were to ask you today the same questions as in the statement, would your answers be the same as in the statement?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Absolutely the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, today you have taken a solemn declaration to tell the truth. Does that mean that we can consider what is contained in the statement to be truthful in nature?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence would tender the statement 1D3876 into evidence along with the associated exhibits that I have sent an e-mail about with a list to all parties last night. I think the number is approximately 44, if I'm doing the math correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, let's first focus on the statement itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The statement, Mr. Registrar, will receive number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D2120, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. We'll deal with the associated exhibit later, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. At this time I would read a summary of the statement, a copy which the booths should have. Andrey Demurenko is a retired Russian army colonel. In addition to the Frunze Military Academy, he also attended American US staff college. He was deployed as a member of the UNPROFOR mission in January 1995 and flew to Zagreb where the General Staff of UN peacekeeping forces was located. Thereafter, he went to Sarajevo where he was the Chief of Staff or first deputy for the commander of Sector Sarajevo until December 1995. He served under three French generals: Generals Gobilliard, de Lapresle, and Bachelet. He found that some 60 per cent of the UN personnel supported the idea that the Serbs were the aggressors because they were presented this by their commanders and the media based on selected facts and were not shown what the Bosnian side was doing. Forty per cent of the UN personnel had their own private opinions but kept quiet about them. French officers would frequently tell Colonel Demurenko in private that they have a different opinion about the war in Bosnia but cannot express it because their orders differ from their private opinions. The French officers thought the main engine for the war was the Bosnian Muslim religious fanaticism and lack of preparedness to accept the Serb position, as well as the illusion of the Bosnian Muslims that they would achieve military support. He found that many UNMO observers were really partial in favour of the Bosnian Muslim side and they informed only about the incoming fire and not the outgoing fire from the Bosnian Muslims, thereby portraying the shelling in Sarajevo as Serb aggression. Also, Pakistani officers would not even collect their own information independently but used what they received from the Bosnian Muslim side. UNPROFOR in Sarajevo had the impression that the Bosnian Muslims were shooting at their own population with snipers, but it was difficult to prove this because the higher command told them to stop such investigations. The ABiH also repeatedly attacked UNPROFOR units. It was clear to Colonel Demurenko that the VRS did not want to destroy either the town of Sarajevo or even the enemy troops in Sarajevo although there was a clear possibility to do so. The life in the Serb side of Sarajevo was exactly the same as in the Muslim part of the city. There were problems with food, water, et cetera. Colonel Demurenko is 100 per cent sure that humanitarian aid to the Muslim side was ending up in black markets. He heard about smuggling of weapons to the Bosnian Muslim side by the humanitarian organisations and UN forces, but these were only rumours and he did not get official information about same. The biggest part of ABiH forces was located in civilian buildings. They had some 20 tanks, five to six mortar batteries, each battery some five to six mortars, both 82-millimetre and 120-millimetre. He saw ABiH units provoke the Serb forces to respond by opening fire and then moving to other locations. The ABiH also had a tunnel under Mount Igman, which was used for transport of troops, humanitarian aid and weapons. After the Markale II explosion in August 1995, the witness went to the scene two hours after the reports of the incident. The investigation was still ongoing when he returned to find that a UN spokesperson, a British colonel, had held a press conference blaming the Serbs for the explosion. There were absolutely no grounds for this as the investigation was ongoing. Colonel Demurenko approached the Sector Sarajevo commander to propose an investigative group headed by himself to investigate the Markale shelling and received approval to do so. Colonel Demurenko and his team went into the field and investigated the source of the shell indicated. The result of the investigation indicated that the Serbs could not have fired the shell in that incident. When he returned with the completed report and photos, he was told by an aide to Commander Bachelet that it was impossible to publish, announce, or give the report to the commander because it differed from the version announced by the UN spokesperson. Colonel Demurenko then organised a press interview where he made public the results of his investigation. Thereafter, he was visited by the BiH army liaison officer, a captain who was the nephew of the Bosnian prime minister, who advised Demurenko that an order had been issued to kill him and that he only had one day do live. He later disagreed with the UNPROFOR BH command G2 officer's report as to the interpretation of Cymbeline radar evidence, saying that it is important to bear in mind that this conclusion is wrong because mortars fired from a middle to long range would have a higher trajectory, not lower, and that the US intelligence officer's conclusion was contradicting the laws of physics when it comes to mortars. In relation to the detention of UN personnel in May to June 1995, Colonel Demurenko stated that the word "hostages" was placed in inverted commas in UN reports because POW could not be used because the UN was supposed to be impair. There was no proper term for the situation so they used hostages, but they weren't really hostages. The ABiH started an offensive, the Serbs responded and were bombed, which was an unjust and partial action by impartial third parties. The Serbs as a result took UNPROFOR soldiers from countries participating in the bombing as POWs. It was a critical point in the war at which point the Muslim side got help from the bombing countries, so it was an adequate response from the Serb side to respond in this way. The term "hostages" is inacceptable. And that completes the public summary. Colonel, I would like to now ask you some additional questions. First if we could turn to page 1 of the written statement, which has now been admitted as D2120. And in paragraph 2, I'd like to look four lines down from the start of that paragraph where it is written, among other things, that you attended a US Staff College. Could you please identify for us which particular American US Staff College you attended and where it is located?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: It was my third stint in higher military education. It's called Command Staff College of the US. The place is Fort Levenworth, the state of Kansas.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how long did that programme last?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: The standard course is one year. I took a bit longer because two months before the beginning of the course, all the officers from other countries had supplementary training, individual training.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And who was among your instructors?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: American trainers, instructors, generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And in this paragraph of your statement, you mention a Ph.D. in military science. Do you have any other advanced degrees in any other field; if so, tell us?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: First of all, the Russian name for a Ph.D. is a candidate for a doctorate in political science, and I completed my education in the team serving the presidential office. I'm a professor of military science of the Russian Federation, and I have occasionally been invited as expert to take part in different scientific seminars and work-shops.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, here the interpretation we've received is that you received a candidate for doctorate in political science. Can you tell us the specific field? Is it military science we're talking about or something else?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: In Russian, it's called candidate in political science, and the chair where I did my training was the chair of national security. It's actually politics in the interests of military science.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in this statement -- pardon me. This statement was taken in 2012. Have you been invited to participate in any lectures or speaking engagements on the topics that you are -- that you have a Ph.D. in or that you are professor in since 2012?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes. All these years, as I've said before, occasionally I've received invitations from Russian or international organisations to take part in work-shops or expert teams or hold lectures on subjects that are interesting to the inviting party, and mainly those have been either peace enforcement operations that actually enforce peace in coercive ways or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the last -- hybrid, hybrid wars.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can call up in e-court 1D5970. And again, I have a hard copy for the usher to show the opposing counsel and then give to the witness if it assists them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, is it the intention of the Prosecution to challenge the qualifications in terms of education and professional experience of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, not in the terms that are being implicated by this particular document, and I'll certainly get into the details of the investigation that was purportedly conducted. But, no, I'm not suggesting he wasn't a candidate for a Ph.D. I'm not suggesting that he hasn't been occasionally invited to participate in various forms. So, no. And I actually was -- I wanted to allow Mr. Ivetic to complete his process, but I was going to object to this as pretty far afield from the relevance of the witness's appearance here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, there seems to be perhaps quite a lot of discussion about the findings this witness made but apparently not on how he was educated, where, and now we know exactly in which fort he was educated, and there he was -- let's try to focus on the matters which are in this dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, Mr. Tieger cross-examined the witness in the Karadzic case, and I respectfully submit that Mr. Tieger attacked the credibility and the impartiality of the witness and therefore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But not -- I do understand not on the basis of being trained well and being educated well but on the content of his expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in some aspects of his training but not with respect to his education in political science or military science such that it got him invited to discussions about the Martens Clause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. And then about the Martens readings, I think that we did read in the briefing note that Mr. Demurenko spoke at the Martens reading and that Judge Pocar also did. Just for full transparency, many of the Judges of the ICTY were present at this occasion, and I can clarify that my colleagues, Moloto and Fluegge, were not there but I was there, so that there is no uncertainty about that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 3 of this document. And here at the top, sir, it is reflected that: "Andrey Demurenko is a former colonel and a veteran of UN peacekeeping operations in the former Yugoslavia. He suggested looking at the problem of access for humanitarian personnel from the point of view of the armed forces. "'Commanders have doubts as to the impartiality of humanitarian workers and we are often unsure about the control exercised over aid,' he explained. 'The ICRC must be the main co-ordinator for all humanitarian organisations providing assistance in armed conflict.'" Is this an accurate summary of what you presented at this Martens reading conference by the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I cannot understand the point of your question. But generally speaking, I stand behind everything I've said before. Everything I've said up to now is absolutely true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the question was whether what was read to you, whether that's an adequate, although very short, summary of what you told when you spoke at the Martens reading. Is it or is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you go into details -- perhaps it's a matter of interpretation. In the interpretation I've heard, it sounded a bit equivocal, as if the Red Cross had humanitarian aid delivered to Sarajevo under its control, and on the other hand, as if I had some information and memories that humanitarian convoys actually delivered also some illegal things, such as weapons for the Bosniaks. You could play this and accuse me of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, no one is accusing you of anything. I read again how your contribution to the Martens reading was summarised. Please tell us whether that is an adequate summary. It's written that you, a former colonel and a veteran of UN peacekeeping operations in the former Yugoslavia, that you suggested looking at the problem of access for humanitarian personnel from the point of view of the armed forces. And then, in quotation marks: "'Commanders have doubts as to the impartiality of humanitarian workers and we are often unsure about the control exercised over aid,' he explained." And then again quotation mark: "'The ICRC must be the main co-ordinator for all humanitarian organisations providing assistance in armed conflict.'" Is that a fair though short summary of what you contributed to the Martens readings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question please, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We would tender this document at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 1D5970 will be Exhibit D2121, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can return to your witness statement, which is D2120, and if we could turn to page 4 of the statement and look at paragraph number 8 together. And again, we need page 4 and focusing on paragraph 8 in the middle. And, sir, in paragraph 8, you describe the duties of a Chief of Staff. And the question I have for you: Did you have any other position or role while deployed in Sarajevo in 1995 in addition to these duties enumerated here as Chief of Staff to Sector Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes. My second position given me by the Russian staff was the commander of the Russian contingent in the former Yugoslavia. That was a small force consisting of the Croatian battalion, the battalion in Bosnia and Herzegovina, one air force squadron, and one smaller unit. Anyway, I was the senior officer of the Russian contingent there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And later in your statement, it's at page 33, and it will be the last part of paragraph 80 that appears on the top of that page. And the last line of that answer says that: "There were 5.000 people under my command and it's impossible to remember all of their names." With respect to these 5.000 people, who were these 5.000 people under your command? Are you talking about the Russian battalion or something else?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: No. This is a reference to the Sector Sarajevo. That unit was over 5.000 strong. That included the French contingent, the Pakistani contingent, and many others. I, as Chief of Staff, was their senior.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could turn to page 7 of the statement and focus on paragraph 14 of the same at the top of the page. And, sir, if we go down four lines from the top, and I can then read the answer that you have given there: "A. Generally speaking, the primary task of any Chief of Staff is to maintain combat readiness of subordinate troops, their preparedness to efficiently operate. That was tactical operation, intelligence, although the word 'intelligence' wasn't used. In Yugoslavia, it was called collection of information ..." Now, I want to ask you, Colonel, when you say in your statement that "intelligence" was not used in Yugoslavia, did anyone ever explain why the word "intelligence" was not used?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Well, it was understandable. We were not a warring party. It was not diplomatic. It was not delicate to use the word "intelligence," and "collecting information" most accurately described the activity that we carried out as a western-type military force.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Colonel, within the UNPROFOR structure, who did the collection of intelligence or, as we have now called it, information?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I just said that. There was a unit or a department or a subunit, G2, that carried out collection of information necessary for UNPROFOR to efficiently function.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Apart from the G2 officers within UNPROFOR, was there anyone who was in an unofficial capacity gathering information or intelligence.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: No, it's not intelligence. It's collection of information. Practically all units of the staff particularly were involved in a way in collecting information, especially military observers. That's natural. They were the eyes and the ears of the contingent, apart from the G2. In addition, there was a department in G3 to -- tactics and operational; G4, logistics; and G5, humanitarian aid. All of them made their small contributions into the general information collection effort that helped manage the process of peacekeeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And apart from the personnel of Sector Sarajevo, was there any knowledge of any other military personnel conducting information reconnaissance?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But many things were not written on paper and couldn't be written on paper, by definition. For instance, we were aware of the activities of some British special forces, the SAS and others, who were involved in in-depth investigation, or G2 units of the US attached to the BH command. I had contacts and friendly relations with them, but I knew that they were not part of the peacekeeping force.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you say "we were aware of the activities of some British special forces," who is the "we" in that sentence?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I mean myself and the staff officers of the Sarajevo Sector; mainly Russian and Ukrainian officers. It was more comfortable between us to share some information that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I see we're at the time for the break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Demurenko, we'll take a break of 20 minutes. We'd like to see you back after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could scroll down a bit on the page and look at paragraph number 16 of your statement, and here, in paragraph 16, you say: "All mass media, journalists, reporters, and my western, (above all English, French, Dutch, and US) colleagues from UNPROFOR and UNMO were spreading rumours that the Serbs were aggressors and that they wanted to destroy the whole of Bosnia. The [sic] idea was unrealistic when I compared it with the situation in the field. Some 60 per cent of the UN personnel supported the idea that the Serbs were the aggressors because they were presented by their commanders and media with only selected facts, but they were not shown what the other, Bosnian Muslim, side was doing. The remaining 40 per cent of the UN personnel had their own opinion but kept quiet about it, and only privately dared to express their differing opinions." That's what's listed here. Now I want to ask you, sir, as to this 60 per cent and 40 per cent statistics, how did you come to this information?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Of course, you have to make a mental balance. I had neither authority nor the possibility to poll anyone, but it was some kind of psychological balance, and I believe it's still true. The balance of opinions that existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how did you reach this psychological balance? What information did you rely upon?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I took all -- into the account all of the information that I had, the reports, the official conversations, the unofficial conversations, the discussions we had between us. To put it briefly, it was the feeling that the majority thought that the Serbs were the aggressors and the rest did not believe that and instead thought it was a civil war where there could be no side that is always right or a side that is always wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. The question was on what basis you made that assessment. What you're now doing is to repeat what you felt that was the case. So you moved away from the question. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we look at the second part of the paragraph, and it will be the last three lines of the paragraph, that we see -- that start off: "It was clear that the opinion of the west was imposed on the UN and was only in one direction - that the Serbs were guilty for everything. This 'correct' opinion was always expressed in UNPROFOR reports that tended to blame the Serbs for the situation in Sarajevo." Can you explain for us what you mean here.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I can. Reading daily reports and sitreps, weekly reports, monthly reports, and comparing that and the details that came in from observation points and other positions of the UNPROFOR, there was an evident disbalance between what was actually going on the ground in the Sector Sarajevo and what was reflected in the documents. For example, what was absolutely unclear was the high amount of shellings or shootings in the column called unknown. For instance, over 24 hours, the Serb side would have shot ten times, the Bosniak side twice, and eight times was unknown. And I asked what makes us unable to establish these unknown sources of shootings or shellings, and the answer was silence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now looking at the very next paragraph, which is number 17, and it starts on this page and goes onto the next page. But in this paragraph, if I can summarise it, you say that French officers frequently told you privately that they had different opinions about the Bosnian war and that the orders they had were differing from their personal opinions. Could you give us an idea of what rank or level of French officers you are talking about here.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes. They would be my rank or a bit lower, colonels, lieutenant-colonels, majors, captains. By the nature of my official duties, I worked with them often and inspected French battalions. That was one of my duties as Chief of Staff, and I had discussions with them. It was not my purpose in doing the inspection to find out their opinion about this balance between Serbs and Bosniaks. That was not my task. But sometimes I came across such opinions, and that's why I reflected it in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could turn to page 8. In paragraph 18, you say: "The French officers thought that the main engine for the war was the Bosnian Muslim religious fanaticism and lack of preparedness to understand and September the other (Serb) ethnic/national opinion and position. The other main reason for the war was the military support to the Bosnian Muslims, or, rather, the Bosnian Muslim illusion that they would get support for their war." My question to you, Colonel: According to the French officers, in relation to these illusions of the Bosnian Muslims that they were going to get military support, from whom did they expect such support to come?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Well, they were not actually illusions. It was quite obvious from the documents, from the facts, and the general course of events that such support was coming in to Bosnian Muslims from the West. It was not my duty to collect information from which parties, France, the US, England. It was not necessary. But the fact that support was being given was completely obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now if we could skip to page 9 and paragraph 22 of the statement. In this paragraph, you talk of a French colonel who was very aggressive, and was -- was against you as a Russian and against the passive policy of General Gobilliard. And in the last three lines of this paragraph, you say: "Every time when he participated in meetings and when the reporting was about the Bosnian Muslim activities, he would deny the Muslim illegal activities. He even silenced some officers when they tried to tell the truth about the fighting in Sarajevo." My first question to you: Do you remember anything else about this particular French colonel? For instance, the exact position that he held.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: (redacted). I remember his face and his behaviour very well. And in passing, I came across information that he appeared before the ICTY as a witness. You can find it in your records, I think. But it's absolutely certain that from the very start, this man was anti-Russian, anti-Serbian, and too aggressive to be present in the US -- in the UN contingent at all. His position was far from impartial.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You have identified him as a deputy commander. Where in the hierarchy did he sit in relation to yourself?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I was also a deputy commander, so he was on the same level as me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did anyone ever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just -- You said that we can find in our records that the person involved appeared before the ICTY as a witness. Can you tell us how did you find out that he appeared as a witness? And was he a protected witness, was he not a protected witness, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't know about his status. I came across his last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us from whom you received the information that the person you had on your mind was a witness in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid to make a mistake now. It could be that I learned from the newspapers or I heard it from my US colleagues with whom I have been keeping in touch about peacekeeping matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic, I'm addressing you. Is there any way that this Chamber -- of course, saying a "French officer," that might not be enough for us to finds out. And where the witness says quite a few things about his attitude, that might be a possibility to verify that on the basis of the evidence of that witness, but we are empty-handed at this moment. Could you assist in any way?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We'll try to do the leg work, but I'm limited by what the witness remembers. Obviously if he cannot give me a name, I can't search for a name. That's why I tried to focus in on his position so that we can then try to see if based upon that information we can find something. But, you know, a lot of people have testified in a lot of cases at this Tribunal, and so it's a rather difficult task to locate someone with just a position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, but I would see our problems are bigger than yours because you can start searching, which we cannot do and do not wish to do. But if you know when he was serving who was the commander, who were the subcommanders, then you might have a clue, and compare that with a list of witnesses and you are aware of. And there are not that many French officers that testified. The Chamber would be assisted by having that information. If the Prosecution would have any clue for us to be better able to understand this portion of the testimony, it would be appreciated as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask the witness. Mr. Demurenko, according to your knowledge and the information you have, did he testify in this case in the Tribunal or just in the Tribunal in any case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought it was quite a long time ago. I think it was in the Slobodan Milosevic case. One of the first cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I ask questions on a slightly different topic, Mr. Ivetic. Sir, you say this gentleman was a deputy commander like yourself. Now, you were the deputy commander for Sector Sarajevo, and you were the Chief of Staff which meant you were the first deputy. Was one of the other deputies after you for Sector Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He wasn't lower than me. He was on the same level. It's like in the US army, in the western armies, even in the Russian army. Under the commander, there are several deputies for different lines of work and a Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There, it was the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to understand. He was also a deputy for -- in Sector Sarajevo? Okay. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, did anyone ever reprimand or punish this French colonel for his behaviour or otherwise bring it up?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. But our conduct is governed by our professional ethical code. That's way it should be. It didn't seem to apply to him, and he wasn't reprimanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we could turn back to page 8 and look at paragraph 20 in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could scroll down a bit. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: After --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you ask this question, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Demurenko, you said "I don't know anything about that," and at the end of your answer you said he wasn't reprimanded. How do you know that he wasn't reprimanded if you don't know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I meant to say is that in my presence at meetings when he made such inadmissible remarks he wasn't reprimanded. But it's quite possible that within the French group after the meeting was over and after I left and after the Pakistanis and Ukrainians left and when the French were left alone, maybe his commander reproached him. But I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the first part of paragraph 20 you talk of a Russian major that you had to send back to Russia because he could not act impartially as to Muslims. Then in the middle of the paragraph, and this will be the fifth line from the beginning of that paragraph, you say: "But on the other hand, many UNMO observers were really partial in favour of the Bosnian Muslim side and they informed only about the incoming fire but not about the outgoing fire by the Bosnian Muslims, thereby portraying the fighting in Sarajevo as a Serb aggression and shelling." And -- so that's what it says. And now I would like to ask you: Could you tell us, first, how did you know about this failure to report the outgoing fire?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: As I said before, by comparing different sources of information, you could see how partial or impartial certain units were. In other words, if we know that there was an artillery shelling in one neighbourhood of Sarajevo and the UNMO report gave a certain figure, whereas the personnel from the check-point gave another figure, and you got a third set of figures from the unit stationed in that neighbourhood, that told you something. You could compare and see how truthful these figures were and how impartial the sources were. I frequently came across such situations that gave me the impression that Bosniak aggression was often kept quiet, under wraps, whereas Serb instances of aggression were put forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, did anyone in the UN structure undertake steps to try to correct this failure of reporting?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I don't know that any radical steps were taken in that direction. All the commanders that I served under at that time, the French generals, did try to enforce the principle of impartiality. They often emphasised that this should be the guiding principles, that the force should be impartial. But these were appeals. But in actual work with the documents, it was not quite clear that it was applied. Documents were used to prove the rightness or wrongness of one of the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you be more precise? You give sweeping statements on all these kinds of things. Do you have a few examples of that, of that documents were used to prove the rightness or wrongness of one of the parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I could answer that question, I would probably have three denunciations on paper. However, you know that in everyday operations you have reports from three different units and you only need to compare them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you can establish if the reports are different that there's an inconsistency in the findings, which is not yet an explanation as to what causes this inconsistencies or discrepancies. There may be a logical explanation; it may be bias, it may be anything. And that's the reason why I asked you whether you have an example or a few examples for us so that we could focus on what the differences are and what may or may not explain them. And, again, irrespective of -- you talked about the rightness or wrongness of one of the parties, so I do not mind which party is treated in a right or in a wrong way. Do you have examples? Do you have such documents which you could show us and say: Look, here you can draw this conclusion; or these three documents, when comparing, show this and this and this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered my -- no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I knew would you have asked me that question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I would have brought such documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I leave it to that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I could perhaps assist Your Honours. One of the paragraphs I wasn't going ask questions about is paragraph 24 of the statement where there is a document that is referenced with an ERN number, which I think is now one of the associated exhibits we have tendered, and we have the witness's description and conclusions in the paragraph and we have the document, and I believe there are several others among the 40-odd that we've tendered that are dealt with in the statement where there are comparisons made of certain language in those documents and the conclusions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just for your information, Mr. Ivetic, this document is not uploaded into e-court by now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is. I did it personally yesterday, so I know it was uploaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was not this morning at 8.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, it was at 8.30 in the evening, so I don't know. But I checked again this morning when I came to the Tribunal at 7.45 and it was. At least on our computers. I don't know if there is a delay between us releasing it and it getting sent because we do have to go through the IT department, but I'll look into that and I'll make sure all documents that I've tendered are released. I did see there was an e-mail about this document and other one from Chambers staff and that's what made me have check and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- that's all I can offer at this point on my feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn together to page 13 of the statement and look at paragraph 36, and in that paragraph you say: "I heard about the smuggling of weapons to the Bosnian Muslim side by the humanitarian organisations and UN forces but they were only rumours and I did not get official information about it." Now, Colonel, I understand that you did not get official information on the topic of smuggling of weapons, but can you tell us or give us any idea about who or what was the source of the rumours that you are relying upon in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Again, I don't have a document. And rumours are rumours. That's what remains in my memory. I have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were the rumours from one person or multiple sources?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Certainly not one person. It's dozens of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. I mean, I thought the witness's clarification was exactly right. There is a difference between sources and rumours and he is indicating, in his earlier response, these are rumours. Now, the question may be aimed at something else, but I think the distinction should be made --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see you had an objection but the answer of the witness satisfied your concerns, if I understand you well. Not about the question but about possible confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would say at this point it's more prophylactic than dealing with an upcoming answer, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to the rumours, can you provide us with any information about the nature of the sources?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Honestly, I'm a military man. And it's not mine to talk about rumours. It's not the kind of person I am. But briefly, I lived there. I heard about me, what people talked. I heard -- I -- I saw weapons held by civilians that they obviously got illegally. It was quite evident that among the people, among civilians, there were a lot of weapons in circulations, but it's not possible now for me to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fair. If we could turn to page 11 of your statement and look at paragraph 30 of the same, and this paragraph starts on this page but goes onto the next page. And here you're talking about the tunnel under Mount Igman. And if you could go through -- go to the top of the next page, the question I want to focus on is the part at the end of this paragraph at the top, which says that: "Yes, it was possible and one could move 500 to 600 troops overnight through the tunnel. So, yes, it was a case of siege but with certain qualifications [sic]?" What was the basis of your information about the tunnel and the number of troops that could be moved through it overnight as in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: As for the tunnel, that question came up many times at our meetings. It was discussed a lot. It's quite obvious the tunnel existed. And it still exists, by the way. It's a museum now in Sarajevo. And the interpretation is not quite correct. It's not under Mount Igman. Its exit was under the airport and the entrance was next to a normal residential house and the exit was next to the airport. Everybody knew. The entire population of Sarajevo knew that the tunnel was being used for different purposes, both for the rotation of troops and for supplies, water, goods, all sorts of things. We even knew the price range for transports during the night, to rent the tunnel for one night. There was a kind of Sarajevo mafia, if you wish, that ran it. But it's obvious that two parties had to be in contact: One at entry points, and the other one at the exit. In my reports, I tried to describe it, but I was not successful. My commanders told me: "Shut up, there is no tunnel. Orders are orders." So there was no tunnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if I may just ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, at page 34, starting from line 6, you were asked about this illegal weapons. You said: "Honestly, I'm a military man. And it's not mine to talk about rumours. It's not the kind of person I am. But briefly, I lived there. I heard about me, what people talked. I heard -- I -- I saw weapons held by civilians that they obviously got illegally." Were you able to determine the ethnicity of these civilians who were carrying these allegedly illegal weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, certainly not. All the more so because I knew there were both Serbs and Muslims in Sarajevo. And Croats. It was a multi-ethnic city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So any of those could have had those illegal weapons. You're not suggesting that they were carried by a specific side only to the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic, I'm trying to follow your suggestions. The documents you uploaded was under what 65 ter number where you said it's -- it was -- I have -- and that's the -- I think the document you referred to which appears in paragraph 24 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. If I can -- my suspicion is that it should be 1D5967.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we check with Mr. Registrar whether that's up uploaded. I tried it under this number. I also tried it 1D05967 and I have no results. Apparently it's unknown in the -- you checked it this morning. Could you perhaps check again?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Not released, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not released. It's uploaded but not released?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't know if this assists or not. But this document is on Defence list twice, once as 1D05967 and also as 1D03900, and it may be it may have been uploaded as the latter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That may assist. I'm pulling it up, but I can't from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can't confirm from there that it is uploaded under the number you -- and released under the number you gave, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can confirm it is uploaded, and now it's not showing up as released. But I can't release it from here. I don't have the privileges on this computer to release documents, but I will get that released at the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently it's uploaded twice. Perhaps you could release the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 3900 has been released. We have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic is not supposed to speak aloud. Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, in relation to the tunnel, you said it was discussed a lot and came up in your meetings. And you said: "My commanders told me: 'Shut up, there is no tunnel. Orders are orders.'" When you say "commanders," to whom are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: All the three of them: General Gobilliard, General Bachelet, and de Lapresle. With each of them I raised this issue, and each of them told me to shut up.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we can turn to page 13 of your statement and look at paragraph 37 of the same. In this paragraph, you talk about the ABiH forces in Sarajevo and you identify that they had some 20 tanks, five to six mortar battery, each battery some five to six mortars, 82-millimetre and 120-millimetre. What was the source for this information on the number of tanks and mortars that the ABiH had in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: It was our job. We had to know the number of troops in different parties. The department G2 principally collected that information, but also it was kept under control by -- it was monitored by all the units, all the monitors, all the observation points, and it was reflected in all the documents in the reports made daily and weekly. There was no secret about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now to switch topics. If with we could turn to page 9 in your statement and look at paragraph 23. And that will be the second paragraph from the top. And here you say: "I met twice with the CNN journalist Christiane Amanpour at the Holiday Inn Hotel and I asked her why she was always propagated against the Serbs, and she told me that it wasn't my business. Many times we in the UNPROFOR had impressions that the Bosnian Muslims were sniping their own population but it was difficult to prove this, because the higher command told us that we should stop this kind of investigation. In addition, in cases of sniper activity it is very difficult to prove the origin of fire, almost impossible to prove whether it was one or the other side who shot from snipers." And so I want to ask you, sir, in relation to UNPROFOR's impression that the Bosnian Muslims were sniping their own population and that the higher command told you to stop investigations, can you identify for us whom you are referring to when you say "higher command"?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I mean my superior officer and mainly the BH Force Commander who is higher than the Sarajevo Sector. They restricted this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you provide us with names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the BH Force Commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I met the BH Force Commander only in the framework of official negotiations. I didn't meet BH Army generals. It was contrary to the principle of impartiality. I'm only talking about the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm talking about the UNPROFOR as well. You said: "I mean my superior officer and mainly the BH Force Commander who is higher than the Sarajevo Sector." I understand your answer that BH Force Commander of UNPROFOR is the person you are referring to. What is his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I meant Sarajevo Sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And who is higher than the Sector Sarajevo? You were referring to a person or a unit higher than the Sarajevo Sector. Who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Once again, above our sector was the UNPROFOR BH command. General Smith was the Force Commander. That's who I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Was he the commander of Sector Sarajevo or of BH command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Was he the commander of Sector Sarajevo or was he the commander of -- the higher command, BH command of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, there is a sector. Above that was the BH force command, and then the UNPROFOR command in Zagreb. Those were the three levels of UNPROFOR Command in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this is exactly why I asked you for names. You provided me with a name of General Smith. Did he hold all these positions, or can you provide me with other names higher than General Smith?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I already gave you an example. The commander of my sector was General Gobilliard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What was your sector?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm repeating. In my sector, Sector Sarajevo, the commanders were General Gobilliard, General de Lapresle, General Bachelet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do I understand your answer that General Smith was higher than the three French generals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we understood each other. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did -- strike that. Was there any reason ever given as to why these type of investigations should be stopped?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Maybe there were reasons in their heads, but they were never voiced at official meetings, and they were never written black on white. What was reflected was the idea of impartiality and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, can you give us an idea of why UNPROFOR had the impression that Bosnian Muslims were sniping their own population?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: To us it was obvious with certain incidents in the streets of Sarajevo. When you saw injured and killed people, it was obvious that they were shot not by the Serbs from the surrounding hills, because by investigating the site of the incident, you saw that there was no area on the Serb side that was a clearing from which you could have shot. There was no clear line of fire for a sniper. They must have been shot by somebody inside the city. However, nobody was going to look for the person who shot. If you want to discuss anti-sniper activity, we can do that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, I have a question here. If you say -- if you looked at it, if you investigate it, is there any document that would demonstrate that on the basis of an incident that it was, as you say, obvious, that the sniping could not have come from the Serb side but must have come from the BiH side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, certainly. In most of the sitreps on shooting incidents, the column source was filled with "unknown." But, at the same time, it was clear that nobody could have shot from the Serbian side -- or, rather, they could have shot but they couldn't have hit because the line of fire was obstructed. But the sitrep showed "unknown," so whoever read that report would think, well, then, who could have shot it? Who could have fired this shot?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if you look at sitreps it may not usually be that clear what line of sight or what line of fire would be possible. So if you say it is reported as unknown source, that you concluded - and it's not clear to me entirely on the basis of what - that it could not have been from the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I meant to say that the formats of sitreps were different. From military observers, we didn't ask a textual description. We wanted a schematic. And it showed the site, the slopes of hills, the depressions, et cetera. From the schematic it was clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I would like to have a look at such a document which would allow for such a conclusion so that that might support and corroborate your evidence. Are you aware or could you produce any such sitrep which would assist us in understanding what you are describing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this minute, I can't. But it's simple, I think. In the archive you have all the reports from military observers including the sketches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just for your information, this Chamber is not dwelling in the archives to find on its own initiative evidence. That's not how it works. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Page 75 of the witness's statement deals with the sitrep that gives grid references for the source of a sniper that wounded a Bosnian civilian coming from Bosnian-held territory. If that assists, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll have a closer look to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mentioned anti-sniping, Colonel. Did UNPROFOR forces in Sector Sarajevo undertake any anti-sniping activities aimed against such Bosnian Muslim snipers operating in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes. I remember when the patients of the Sarajevo Sector Command Staff ran out, I was able to persuade the commander to establish an anti-sniping group or anti-sniping groups. The French army has a fantastic weapon, a sniping weapon, that is much better and stronger than the SVD rifle used by the warring parties. It is stronger than 7.62 millimetres that the warring parties used, and this weapon was perfectly able to counter the snipers that were nested inside Sarajevo buildings. These groups were established. They efficiently fought with the snipers. And I'm sorry now, but I don't remember the exact number of the targets that we neutralized because it's not mostly about the snipers that we killed but it was about a demonstration of the resolve of the Sarajevo Sector command to fight sniping. And in the area at least where I was the initiator, we managed to reduce sniping activities many times by Autumn 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to show you a document that is marked 1D7014, and I have a hard copy again for the usher to show opposing counsel and then provide to the witness if it assists. And while you wait for the hard copy, perhaps we can work with what is on the screen. We have before us a document and it is from the foreign military studies office and its author is LTC John E. Sray, US army. First of all, are you familiar with either the author or the foreign military studies office that is identified in this document? Colonel? I don't know if you've received translation. Are you familiar with the author, Colonel Sray, or the foreign military studies office? That was the question.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: No, I don't know him personally. I came across this article much later, one or two years after the completion of my mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 3 of this document, and I would like to focus on the second-to-last paragraph on that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, do you want Mr. Ivetic to first phrase his question or would you already intervene now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I think I would like a chance to intervene before the question is asked in part I think because I think this is -- I can't imagine how under the circumstances that have unfolded, and I was waiting to see how the document might be used, I think at a minimum this is going to be a leading question, look at what somebody else said, and is that consistent with whatever. That's a leading process. Secondly, I think the nature of this document, which is sort of an opinion piece, it had nothing to do with this witness. And that is, as we can see from the sources for the piece, relatively -- I mean, this particular section is sourced on one newspaper article. I don't think it assists this process at all. Not with a fact witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, when phrasing your question, would you please keep in mind to refrain from leading because Mr. Tieger has some concerns about that. And I further notice that also in earlier questions, you sometimes ask the witness to give comment on the opinion of others. Now it's already problematic now and then to hear a witness of fact expressing opinions, but it sometimes becomes even more problematic if he is opining on opinions of others. Would you please keep all this in mind when you phrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Although, I think that we've been dealing with the witness's statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, please do it -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- so I don't know how other opinions of others has come into the direct thus far since -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I can find it for you if you insist. I'll do that during the break. But I'd first like to hear how you phrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You've told us about the anti-sniping activities that you undertook in Sector Sarajevo. In the second-to-last paragraph of this document, the author has written as follows about the anti-sniping activities. And my question to you, after I read that selection, would be simply to ask you if this comports with what you have been talking about the anti-sniping activities and your experiences in Sarajevo or not. And the part that I'm focusing on is the part that reads: "Anti-sniping activities conducted by the UN Protection Force, UNPROFOR, in Sarajevo, in fact, constitute quite impressive operations. Teams which perform this duty receive exceptional training from their armies and possess state-of-the-art optical aids and equipment. Employing these capabilities, the French recently decided to test over three years' worth of UN hunches pertaining to this issue. Their investigation 'definitively' (their words) established the validity of UN suppositions that 'some' gun-fire came from Bosniak government soldiers deliberately shooting at their own civilians."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, again I object. This is a leading question. Instead of eliciting what this witness knows or purports to have known at the time, now we present him with something said by somebody else, who as far as I can tell wasn't there but is simply writing an opinion piece based solely on a newspaper article that he read, and now we're asked -- is -- presented to this witness to affirm that and is fed this information to affirm. That's a leading question, I'm afraid. It's a little different when we're talking about contemporaneous documents relating to what this witness was involved with at the time, so this process I fear has the -- sort of the converging flaws of both leading and delving into irrelevant information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the transcript -- the transcript stops at the quote Mr. Ivetic gave. Not yet a question is on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I -- for transparency, I gave my question before I read the quote, Your Honour, and that should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. That's at the beginning the page 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And it's in relation to the evidence that I led, that rather significant evidence that the witness himself told us about the anti-sniping of the French that he organised, and I'm simply asking for this contemporaneous document written shortly after the events in question, written by somebody who was in Bosnia, as Mr. Tieger knows, since that was in the submissions that this is a former aide of General Rose. So the submissions of the Prosecution have been incorrect and I would say false as to those points, because this is a contemporaneous document and I'm testing the reliability of this document based upon what the witness just told us about to see if we can find more information. The Prosecution has been permitted time and again, particularly in the last few months of witnesses, to provide documents to witnesses that the witness says I know nothing about this document and they have been introduced into evidence. One example was the bullet that was introduced through Dr. Stankovic where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- it's just shown to the witness and it's introduced into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the witness may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, I forgot the question by now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, a portion was read to you of an article and the question -- let me just check because I have a little bit of a problem with my computer. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can I take over?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
